analysis.one_liner: Requires insurance to cover autoimmune and blood disorder drugs and limits repeat prior authorization.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in three House committees since its June 2026 introduction with one bipartisan cosponsor and no vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require group and individual health plans to cover drugs prescribed for autoimmune diseases, hemophilia, and Von Willebrand disease, whether dispensed by a pharmacy or given in a doctor's office. It would also stop insurers from requiring prior authorization for those drugs more than once every 12 months, with narrow exceptions for short-term drugs and certain risky medications. Patients on expensive specialty drugs often face repeated approval fights each year; this would make coverage of those drugs automatic and the approval paperwork annual at most.
analysis.who_benefits: People with autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and Crohn's disease, and people with hemophilia or Von Willebrand disease, who currently may face prior-authorization requests multiple times per year for the same drug and coverage fights over whether a drug is covered when dispensed by a pharmacy versus given in a clinic. Their families and employers also benefit from fewer interruptions in treatment.

how_it_helps.text: Requires all group and individual plans to cover drugs indicated for autoimmune diseases, hemophilia, or Von Willebrand disease, whether dispensed by a pharmacy or furnished incident to another service, closing a common coverage gap between medical and pharmacy benefits.

Bars insurers from requiring prior authorization for these drugs more than once in any 12-month period, so a patient whose drug is approved does not have to re-win approval repeatedly for the same ongoing treatment.

Carves out narrow exceptions where repeated authorization remains allowed: drugs typically used for 12 months or less, opioids, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, carisoprodol, and drugs subject to an FDA risk management program.

Applies the requirements uniformly across employer plans governed by ERISA, the Internal Revenue Code, and individual and group market plans under the Public Health Service Act, starting with plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2027.

analysis.who_pays: Health plans and insurers bear the cost of covering these drugs without repeated authorization, including expensive biologics and blood-clotting factors that can cost thousands to tens of thousands of dollars per patient per month. Those costs are expected to flow into premiums paid by enrollees and employers. Insurers and pharmacy benefit managers also lose a utilization-management tool. Patients would still pay whatever cost-sharing their plan sets; the bill does not cap deductibles or coinsurance for these drugs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, employers, and enrollees through premiums

drawbacks.text: Requiring coverage of every drug indicated for autoimmune disease, including high-cost biologics, without cost-sharing limits could raise premiums for all enrollees, since the expense of treating a small number of patients on very expensive drugs is spread across everyone in the plan.

Limiting prior authorization to once per year removes a tool insurers use to steer patients to preferred or lower-cost alternatives first, which insurers argue keeps drug spending in check; without it, plans may cover less preferred, higher-priced drugs by default.

The bill mandates coverage but does not cap patient cost-sharing, so a patient could still owe large deductible or coinsurance amounts for these drugs even after coverage and authorization rules change.
Being referred to three committees, the bill would need coordinated action from Ways and Means, Education and Workforce, and Energy and Commerce to advance, a procedural burden few House bills clear.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient benefit is real and targeted: people with chronic autoimmune diseases and bleeding disorders would no longer face repeated authorization battles for the same ongoing treatment, and coverage would be guaranteed regardless of how the drug is delivered. The costs are also real but familiar from prior federal coverage mandates: higher premiums spread across enrollees, and less insurer control over which costly drugs get used first. The bill is narrow and well-defined rather than sweeping, which limits both sides of the ledger.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in June 2026 and referred to three House committees, where it has sat with no hearings, markup, or floor vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Julie Johnson of Texas introduced the bill on June 8, 2026, joined by Mr. Lawler, making it a bipartisan introduction with one Republican cosponsor.

The Speaker referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and additionally to the Committees on Education and Workforce and Ways and Means, meaning all three would need to act on the parts in their jurisdiction.
The action history shows no further steps after the referral: no committee markup, no hearing, and no floor vote as of the latest record.
The bill applies to plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2027, which falls within the current Congress, so it could still move before that date if a committee schedules it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no outcome has been reached; health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers retain the current prior-authorization practices for autoimmune and blood disorder drugs, while patients have gained nothing yet. The bill's own momentum favors its sponsors only in the limited sense that a bipartisan introduction exists on the record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, for now; no one else yet

for.name: Rep. Julie Johnson
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce jurisdiction member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring coverage and limiting prior authorization for autoimmune and blood disorder drugs.

for.name: Rep. Mike Lawler
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its first and only cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by one Democrat and one Republican, and the full cosponsor list shows a single Republican, so partisan lines have not yet formed around it either way.

industries.note: Insurers would lose the ability to demand prior authorization more than once a year for autoimmune and blood disorder drugs and would be required to cover them however they are dispensed. Their cost in premiums is the patient benefit in fewer treatment interruptions.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and utilization-management vendors
industries.note: These firms earn fees administering prior-authorization reviews; an annual limit on repeat authorizations for this drug class shrinks that business for millions of chronic-disease patients.

Guaranteed coverage of drugs indicated for autoimmune diseases, hemophilia, and Von Willebrand disease, without repeated authorization, protects the market for expensive biologics and clotting factors. Patients benefit from the same guarantee, though the bill does not restrain drug prices.
Employers who fund their own plans would face the same coverage mandate and annual authorization limit, raising expected costs, while employees with these conditions get steadier treatment.

analysis.trajectory: With two sponsors, a referral split across three committees, and no action in the record since June 2026, this bill follows the typical path of late-session single-sponsor health mandates: it would need one committee chair to schedule a markup and then Speaker approval to reach the floor, and none has occurred. Absent a push from committee leadership or a larger vehicle, it is likely to expire at the end of this Congress without a vote.
